title: Journey to the Space Station
summary: A Grade 5 student wins a school essay contest and gets to video-call a real astronaut aboard the International Space Station, learning about microgravity and the research done there.
poll: Doing scientific research aboard the International Space Station is worth the time and money it costs.

versions.title: Journey to the Space Station
versions.text:
Lama likes space. She is in Grade 5. Her class had a contest. Kids wrote about space.

Lama wrote a lot. She wrote well. She won! The prize was big.

She got to talk to an astronaut. The astronaut was way up high. She was on a space station.

On the big day, the class sat in the hall. They saw a big screen. Dr. Huda was on it! She was far away, up in space.

Lama asked, "How do you sleep up there?" Dr. Huda said, "I float! It is not like here."

Food floats, too. Dr. Huda eats from small bags. If she lets go, it can float away!

Dr. Huda looks at plants up there. This can help us one day.

Lama was so happy. She wants to go to space, too!

versions.title: Journey to the Space Station
versions.text:
Lama likes space a lot. She is a student in Grade 5. Her school held a contest about space.

Lama wrote about the stars and the planets. She worked hard. She won the contest! The prize was something big.

She would get to talk with a real astronaut. The astronaut lived on a space station. It flies high above the Earth.

On the big day, the whole class sat in the school hall. They watched a big screen at the front. Dr. Huda showed up on the screen. She was far away, up in space!

Lama asked her first question. "How do you sleep up there?" Dr. Huda smiled. She said, "I float while I sleep! There is only a little gravity in space."

Dr. Huda also eats food from small bags. If she lets go of her food, it can float right in front of her face!

Dr. Huda studies plants on the space station. This work might help people on Earth someday.

Lama felt proud of herself. She wants to be a scientist when she grows up. Maybe she will fly to space one day too!

versions.title: Journey to the Space Station
versions.text:
Lama has always loved space, from the stars to the far planets. She is a student in Grade 5 at her school. This year, her school held a contest about space. Every student in her class had to enter.

Lama wrote her essay about the stars, the moon, and the planets. She worked hard on every line, picking her best ideas and facts. In the end, she won the contest! The prize was more exciting than she had ever imagined.

As the winner, Lama would get to talk, live, with a real astronaut. The astronaut, Dr. Huda, lived and worked aboard the International Space Station. It circles the Earth high above the clouds. It makes one full trip around the planet about every ninety minutes.

On the big day, the whole class gathered in the school hall to watch. They stared at a large screen at the front of the room. Dr. Huda appeared on the screen, smiling and waving. She was orbiting far above them, hundreds of kilometers up in space!

Lama asked her first question. "How do you sleep up there?" Dr. Huda explained that she floats while she sleeps, zipped inside a bag strapped to the wall. Up on the station, there is only a tiny bit of gravity. Scientists call this microgravity. Almost everything floats unless it is tied down.

Dr. Huda showed the class something fun. She let a tiny drop of water float out of its pouch. Instead of falling, it curled into a little ball, drifting gently in the air.

Dr. Huda explained that she also does research on the station. She studies how plants grow without much gravity, and how space affects muscles and bones. This research could help astronauts stay healthy on future trips to the Moon and Mars.

Lama felt proud once the call ended, and Dr. Huda's story had inspired her. She told her teacher that she wants to become a scientist, or maybe even an astronaut. Someday, she hopes, she might fly to space herself.

versions.title: Journey to the Space Station
versions.text:
Lama has always been fascinated by everything connected to space, from the twinkling stars overhead to the faraway, mysterious planets. She is a student in Grade 5 at her school in Saudi Arabia, and this year her school held a writing contest about space that every student in her class was required to enter.

Lama wrote her essay about the stars, the moon, and the planets in our solar system. She worked hard on every sentence, carefully choosing her best ideas and most interesting facts, and in the end, she won the contest! The prize turned out to be far more exciting than she had ever imagined it could be.

As the winner, Lama would get to speak, live, with a real astronaut. The astronaut, Dr. Huda, lived and worked aboard the International Space Station, a research station that circles the Earth high above the clouds, completing one full trip around the planet roughly every ninety minutes.

On the big day, Lama's entire class gathered in the school hall to watch. They stared eagerly at a large screen set up at the front of the room. Suddenly, Dr. Huda appeared on the screen, smiling warmly and waving. She was orbiting far above them, hundreds of kilometers up in space!

Lama asked her first question. "How do you sleep up there?" Dr. Huda smiled and explained that she floats while she sleeps, zipped inside a sleeping bag strapped firmly to the wall. Up on the station, there is only a tiny amount of gravity, a condition scientists call microgravity, so almost everything floats unless it is tied down carefully.

Dr. Huda showed the class something delightful. She let a tiny drop of water drift out of its pouch, and instead of falling the way it would on Earth, it curled into a perfect little ball, drifting gently in the air in front of the camera.

Dr. Huda explained that she also carries out important research aboard the station. She studies how plants grow without much gravity, and how living in space for many months affects astronauts' muscles and bones, since both can weaken when they are not used against gravity. Scientists hope this research will help astronauts stay healthy on future missions to the Moon and even Mars.

Lama felt incredibly proud of herself once the call finally ended, and Dr. Huda's journey had deeply inspired her. She told her teacher that she wants to become a scientist, or perhaps even an astronaut herself, when she grows up. Someday, she hopes, she might travel to space herself and look back down at the Earth.

versions.title: Journey to the Space Station
versions.text:
Lama had always been fascinated by everything connected to space, from the twinkling stars overhead to the faraway, mysterious planets she read about in books. As a student in Grade 5 at her school in Saudi Arabia, she was thrilled when her school announced a writing contest about space, one that every student in her class was required to enter.

Lama wrote her essay about the stars, the moon, and the planets in our solar system, weaving in several surprising facts she had discovered while researching in the library. She worked diligently on every sentence, carefully selecting her strongest ideas, and in the end, she won the contest. The prize turned out to be far more exciting than she had ever imagined it could be.

As the winner, Lama would get to speak, live, with a real astronaut. The astronaut, Dr. Huda, lived and worked aboard the International Space Station, a research station roughly the size of a football field that orbits the Earth at an altitude of about 400 kilometers, completing one full trip around the planet every ninety minutes while traveling at nearly 28,000 kilometers per hour.

Dr. Huda explained that becoming an astronaut requires many years of dedicated work. She studied engineering at university, then spent years training in simulators that recreate, or simulate, the conditions of space travel, learning how to fly spacecraft, repair broken equipment, and respond calmly to emergencies, before she was finally selected for her mission.

On the big day, Lama's entire class gathered in the school hall to watch. They stared eagerly at a large screen set up at the front of the room. Suddenly, Dr. Huda appeared on the screen, smiling warmly and waving. She was orbiting far above them, hundreds of kilometers up in space!

Lama asked her first question: "How do you sleep up there?" Dr. Huda smiled and explained that she floats while she sleeps, zipped inside a sleeping bag strapped firmly to the wall. Aboard the station, there is only a tiny amount of gravity, a condition scientists call microgravity, so almost everything floats unless it is tied down carefully.

Dr. Huda showed the class something delightful. She let a tiny drop of water drift out of its pouch, and instead of falling the way it would on Earth, it curled into a perfect little ball, drifting gently in the air in front of the camera, wobbling slightly with every small movement of the station.

Dr. Huda explained that she also carries out important experiments aboard the station. One experiment examines how plants grow without much gravity, while another studies how living in space for many months can cause muscle atrophy and weaker bones, since the body does not need to work as hard against gravity. Scientists hope these experiments will help future astronauts sustain their health on long missions to the Moon and even Mars.

Lama felt incredibly proud of herself once the call finally ended. She told her teacher that she wants to become a scientist, or perhaps even an astronaut herself, when she grows up. Someday, she hopes, she might journey to space herself and look back down at the Earth below.

When her school in Saudi Arabia announced a writing contest about space that every student in her class was required to enter, she felt an immediate surge of excitement.

Lama wrote her essay about the stars, the moon, and the planets in our solar system, weaving in several surprising facts she had uncovered while researching diligently in the library, carefully selecting her strongest ideas; in the end, she won the contest, and the prize turned out to be far more exciting than she had ever dared to imagine.

As the winner, Lama would get to speak, live, with a real astronaut. The astronaut, Dr. Huda, lived and worked aboard the International Space Station, a research station approximately the size of a football field that orbits the Earth at an altitude of about 400 kilometers, completing one full circuit of the planet every ninety minutes while traveling at nearly 28,000 kilometers per hour.

Dr. Huda explained that becoming an astronaut requires many years of dedicated effort; she studied engineering at university, then spent years training in simulators that recreate, or simulate, the demanding conditions of space travel, learning how to pilot spacecraft, repair malfunctioning equipment, and respond calmly to emergencies, before she was finally selected for her mission.

Lama felt incredibly proud of herself once the call finally ended. She told her teacher that she aspires to become a scientist, or perhaps even an astronaut herself, when she grows up, and that someday, she hopes, she might journey to space herself and gaze back down at the Earth below.

versions.title: Journey to the Space Station
versions.text:
Lama, a Grade 5 student at her school in Saudi Arabia, had always been fascinated by everything connected to space, from the twinkling stars overhead to the distant, mysterious planets she encountered in library books; when her school announced a writing contest requiring every student in her class to submit an essay about space, she poured herself into the project, weaving in surprising facts she had uncovered through careful research and selecting her strongest ideas with unusual diligence for a student her age. Her effort paid off: she won the contest, and the prize proved far more thrilling than anything she had dared to imagine.

The prize was a live conversation with Dr. Huda, an astronaut living and working aboard the International Space Station, a research outpost ranking among the largest human-made structures ever assembled in orbit and built jointly by engineers and astronauts from several countries; roughly the size of a football field, the station orbits the Earth at an altitude of about 400 kilometers, completing a full circuit of the planet every ninety minutes while traveling at nearly 28,000 kilometers per hour. Becoming an astronaut, Dr. Huda later explained, demands years of dedicated effort: after studying engineering at university, she spent years training in simulators that recreate the conditions of space travel, learning to pilot spacecraft, repair malfunctioning equipment, and respond calmly to emergencies, before finally being selected for her mission.

On the appointed day, Lama's entire class gathered in the school hall and watched eagerly as Dr. Huda appeared on a large screen, smiling and waving from hundreds of kilometers above them; Lama's first question concerned sleep, and Dr. Huda explained that she floats through the night, zipped inside a sleeping bag strapped firmly to the wall, since the station's gravity amounts to only about one-millionth of what people feel on Earth, a condition scientists call microgravity that leaves nearly everything floating unless it is deliberately secured.

To illustrate the effect, Dr. Huda released a tiny drop of water from its pouch; rather than falling as it would on Earth, it curled into a perfect sphere, drifting and wobbling gently in front of the camera with every small movement of the station. She went on to describe the important experiments she conducts aboard the station, including one that examines how plants grow without substantial gravity and another that studies how extended time in space can cause muscle atrophy and diminished bone density, since the body need not work as hard against gravity; scientists hope such experiments will help future astronauts sustain their health during long missions to the Moon and even Mars, demonstrating how research conducted far from Earth can still address challenges that affect life back home.

Lama felt immensely proud once the call ended, and she told her teacher that she now hoped to become a scientist, or perhaps even an astronaut herself, when she grew up; the experience taught her something she would not soon forget, namely that reaching for an extraordinary dream, whether it involves a space station circling the planet or a goal much closer to home, begins with ordinary habits of curiosity, careful work, and patience practiced day after day.

LOW.prompt: Would you like to talk to a real astronaut like Lama did? Explain why or why not, using at least two facts from the story.

I used at least two facts from the story.
I wrote complete sentences with capital letters and periods.
LOW.modelAnswer: Yes, I would like to talk to a real astronaut like Lama did. I would want to ask how astronauts sleep, because Dr. Huda floats inside a sleeping bag strapped to the wall. I would also want to see how food floats, since there is very little gravity in space. I think it would be amazing to see all of that for myself.

keyWords.definition: a condition with very little gravity, so things and people float

keyWords.definition: careful study done to learn new facts about something

keyWords.definition: a short piece of writing about one topic

keyWords.definition: to make someone want to do or create something
keyWords.example: The coach's speech inspired the team to try harder.

keyWords.definition: the curved path something follows as it circles a planet or star
keyWords.example: The moon moves in an orbit around the Earth.

MID.prompt: Explain how Dr. Huda's research on the space station might help people in the future. Use at least two details from the story.
checklist: I explained how the research could help people.
I used at least two details from the story.
I organized my ideas in a clear order.
MID.modelAnswer: Dr. Huda's research could help people in a few ways. She studies how plants grow without much gravity, which could teach scientists new things about growing food. She also studies how living in space for a long time affects astronauts' bodies, since muscles and bones can get weaker. This research could help future astronauts stay healthy on long trips to the Moon or Mars.

keyWords.definition: the weakening or shrinking of a muscle from lack of use
keyWords.example: Doctors told the patient to walk daily to prevent muscle atrophy after the injury.

keyWords.definition: to create conditions that copy something real, usually for study or practice
keyWords.example: Pilots simulate storms in a flight trainer before flying in real bad weather.

keyWords.definition: to keep something going or support it over time

keyWords.definition: an important job or trip done for a special purpose
keyWords.example: The team planned every step of their mission to the mountain's summit.

keyWords.definition: a scientific test done to learn something new
keyWords.example: In our science experiment, we checked which plant grew fastest in sunlight.

wrong.B: The story does not connect this research to choosing astronauts.

wrong.B: The story does not say water is scarce.

HIGH.prompt: Dr. Huda said becoming an astronaut takes many years of hard work. Do you think the effort is worth it? Support your argument with evidence from the story.
checklist: I supported my position with specific evidence from the story.
I addressed at least one point someone might make against my view.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I think the years of hard work are worth it. Dr. Huda's training let her fly real spacecraft, fix equipment, and handle emergencies, skills that keep her and her crew safe. Her experiments on muscle atrophy and plant growth could help future astronauts survive missions to the Moon and Mars, which shows her work matters beyond her own career. Someone might argue that many years of training is too long to wait, but important discoveries, like how to keep humans healthy far from Earth, often take patient, careful study.
